== Biography ==

Alice is a thoughtful and curious observer of Wonderland. She has read about institutions of justice in books and takes quiet pride in her education, reflecting that very few girls of her age would understand such formal vocabulary as "jurors." When brought to a court trial, she observes the judge, jury-box, and other furnishings with the satisfaction of recognizing what she has learned from her reading.

She conducts her inquiries with a mixture of boldness and restraint. When the gardeners puzzle her by painting white roses red, she approaches to watch them and asks timidly why they labor at this curious task. At a tea party, when told there was no room for her, she declared indignantly that plenty of room remained and seated herself in a large armchair. Yet she can be gentle and attentive with those she meets; when she encounters the Duchess again after an earlier meeting in the kitchen, she notes that the Duchess's temper has grown pleasant and walks with her.

Alice reflects on what she has observed. Regarding the Duchess's earlier harshness, she wonders whether pepper—present in the kitchen where they had met before—might have been the source of that savage mood. She herself thinks that were she a Duchess, she would keep no pepper in her kitchen at all. When she meets the Mock Turtle and Gryphon, and they speak of the Lobster Quadrille, Alice carefully notes that she has never lived under the sea, has not been introduced to a lobster, and has never tasted one—details that help explain why the underwater dance is so foreign to her understanding.

Alice moves through Wonderland with a peculiar composure, asking genuine questions about what puzzles her and attending to the answers with perfect seriousness. She does not shy from contradiction; when she believes herself right, she speaks loudly and decidedly, standing her ground even as the world around her behaves quite otherwise.

== Narrative role ==

Alice joins an afternoon tea party with the March Hare, Hatter, and Dormouse, declaring indignantly that there is plenty of room despite their protests, and settling herself in a large arm-chair. She next observes gardeners painting white roses red—a curious sight that draws her nearer. Approaching them timidly, she asks why they are engaged in this work. The gardeners explain that they mistakenly planted a white rose-tree instead of a red one, and they fear the Queen's punishment if she discovers their error.

Later, Alice encounters the Duchess, who greets her warmly and affectionately links her arm through Alice's. Finding the Duchess in an unexpectedly pleasant temper, Alice wonders whether pepper from the kitchen might have been responsible for the Duchess's earlier savagery. The Duchess becomes preoccupied with discovering moral lessons in everything, testing Alice's patience. When Alice ventures to suggest that perhaps there is no moral to be found, the Duchess sharply dismisses her: "Tut, tut, child!"

Alice subsequently meets the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon, conversing with them about the Lobster Quadrille, an elaborate underwater dance. When asked if she has lived beneath the sea, she denies it; when asked whether she has ever tasted or been introduced to a lobster, she checks herself and carefully says "No, never."

Alice's final observed moment finds her at a trial of the Knave of Hearts. Though she has never attended a court of justice before, she has read about them in books and takes satisfaction in identifying nearly every element by its proper name. She notes the King presiding as judge, uncomfortably wearing both crown and great wig. She observes the White Rabbit carrying trumpet and parchment, a large dish of tarts upon the table, and the jury-box containing twelve creatures—some animals, some birds. She feels particular pride in knowing the word "jurors," believing that few girls her age would understand its meaning.

== Personality ==

Alice exhibits a distinctive combination of curiosity and restraint. She is observant, inclined to go nearer to watch the gardeners engaged in their mysterious work, and takes genuine interest in understanding the unusual scenes around her. Yet this curiosity is tempered by caution and politeness—when questioning the gardeners about the roses, she speaks "a little timidly." She possesses an underlying assertiveness that surfaces when provoked, declaring with indignation that "There's plenty of room!" despite being told otherwise. This willingness to contradict those around her stands in tension with her general deference.

Alice is self-aware and reflective. She takes pride in her knowledge, pleased to recognize objects in a court of justice and turning a newly learned word over in her mind with satisfaction. She demonstrates intellectual honesty—when speaking with the Mock Turtle, she catches herself before exaggerating and chooses to speak truthfully instead. This capacity for self-correction suggests a conscience at work beneath her childlike wonder. She is also capable of warmth; when the Duchess greets her with affection, Alice reciprocates the sentiment gladly.

Her manner of thinking is both orderly and imaginative. Faced with unfamiliar situations, she draws upon what she has read in books to make sense of the world, and when idle, she finds occupation in observing and analyzing her surroundings rather than in distress. This suggests a mind inclined toward learning and understanding, even in the face of bewilderment.

== Relationships ==

'''[[Gryphon]]''' — acquaintance. Alice seems to regard the Gryphon's company as preferable to being exposed to greater dangers in Wonderland.

'''[[White Rabbit]]''' — acquaintance. Alice appears to regard the White Rabbit with hesitation and deference, approaching with a timid voice when they meet.

'''[[Cheshire Cat]]''' — acquaintance. Alice calls the Cheshire Cat "a friend of mine" and values its company as "somebody to talk to" amid her bewildering surroundings.

'''[[Mock Turtle]]''' — acquaintance. Alice seems to observe the Mock Turtle with curiosity and sympathy as it recounts the tale of the Lobster Quadrille.

'''[[Queen]]''' — adversary. Alice seems to regard the Queen with apprehension, aware of its dangerous temperament, yet speaks "very loudly and decidedly" in direct contradiction when provoked.

== Trivia ==

Alice is a little girl of considerable learning, as she herself reflected when she recognized the name "jurors" during the trial of the Knave of Hearts. She repeated the word several times over, being rather proud of it, for she thought and rightly so that very few little girls of her age knew its meaning. She had prepared for her first encounter with a court of justice by reading about such proceedings in books, which left her pleased to discover she could identify nearly everything there: the judge by his great wig, the jury-box, and the twelve creatures who comprised the jury.

Curious by nature, Alice is given to careful observation and introspection. When she discovered gardeners painting white roses red, she found the sight so peculiar that she approached them to ask the reason for such an undertaking. She reflected thoughtfully on her previous meeting with the Duchess in the kitchen, wondering whether pepper had caused that lady's savage temper, and resolved that when she herself became a Duchess, she would keep no pepper in her kitchen whatsoever.

Alice has never lived under the sea, nor has she been introduced to a lobster, facts she took care to affirm when the Mock Turtle questioned her experience with such matters.
